title: Death without fear
hook: death is part of the order; the one who remembers is not afraid

segments.voice: Yesterday, why suffering: pain as the bitter medicine, never pretended away. Your line was pain, honestly. Did you give one true answer instead of fine? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

Clean sheets on the guest bed. A towel folded at the foot of the bed. Everyone in the house knows two things about the guest: they're welcome, and they're leaving. Nobody is shocked when the bag gets packed. That's simply what a guest does. The Guru Granth Sahib reaches for pictures like this one: the world as a place we stay for a while, and leaving as part of the visit. It isn't easy dinner talk, and the Gurus speak about it calmly anyway. Death without fear.
screen: `A GUEST ROOM, MADE UP.` → `WELCOME, AND LEAVING.` → `DEATH WITHOUT FEAR.`

segments.voice: First, the order. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak says it in a few plain words. In paraphrase: whoever has come will go; each one's turn comes. Not a threat. A description. Death is inside the Hukam, the order of things, like sunset is inside the day. Second, a surprising request. In a hymn in Raag Vadahans, sung at the time of mourning, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: don't call death bad, people, if you know how to truly die. That's a strange thing to ask at a funeral. He isn't saying grief is wrong; the same hymns are full of tears. He's saying death itself isn't the enemy. The question is how a life has been lived, and whether it was lived remembering. Third, Kabir goes further. In one of his couplets in the Granth he says, in paraphrase: the death the whole world fears fills my mind with joy, because in dying one meets the One who is perfect bliss. Some readers hear two deaths in that line: the death of the body, and the daily dying of the swollen self. Kabir seems at home with both. Fourth, the fearless one. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, names the One as nirbhau, without fear. The Gurus' teaching is that a person who keeps remembering the fearless One begins to share in that fearlessness. Fear may still come. It just stops being the thing remembered. Which brings back the guest room: welcome while the visit lasts, and not shocked when the bag is packed. The sheets were clean for a guest who was always going to leave, and that never made the welcome less.
screen: `WHOEVER HAS COME WILL GO.` · `DON'T CALL DEATH BAD.` · `KABIR: THE DEATH THE WORLD FEARS.` · `NIRBHAU: REMEMBER THE FEARLESS ONE.` · then, large: `UNAFRAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe calmly with the thought of it. Go gently; if this subject is raw for you right now, simply breathe and rest instead. Settle. Let the thought come, quietly: this life is a visit. On the in-breath, notice you are here, alive, welcome. On the out-breath, let the leaving be part of it, without forcing anything. If fear rises, don't fight it; just let the breath keep going. If you pray, you can hold the word nirbhau, without fear, in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Death without fear. Death is part of the Lord's order, and the Gurus teach that the one who remembers the fearless One need not be ruled by fear of it. Today's word.

Your line: unafraid. Today, notice one small fear that's been steering you, and ask whether it deserves the wheel. Then do the thing it's been keeping you from. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: At a Sikh death, family and sangat gather for kirtan and Ardas, the evening prayer Kirtan Sohila is recited, and a reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is often held; Sikh teaching discourages loud lamenting while honoring grief.
